title: How I Made My Spring Boot DTOs Immutable Using Java Records and ModelMapper
author: Niaz Bin Siraj
excerpt: Learn how to make your Spring Boot DTOs immutable using Java Records and ModelMapper. Discover the benefits of immutability and how to fix ModelMapper's lack of record support with a single module.
contents:
As a Java developer, I am always looking for ways to improve my code quality. Recently, while working on a Spring Boot REST API, I came across an intriguing idea: DTOs must be immutable. This got me thinking - why should DTOs be immutable, and how can I achieve this cleanly in my Spring Boot application?

The Problem with Mutable DTOs

Initially, I was using traditional Java POJOs for my DTOs, with getters and setters, and mapping them to my JPA entities using ModelMapper.

A typical DTO looked something like this:

public class UserDTO {
    private String name;
    private String email;

    public UserDTO() {}

    public String getName() {
        return name;
    }

    public void setName(String name) {
        this.name = name;
    }

    public String getEmail() {
        return email;
    }

    public void setEmail(String email) {
        this.email = email;
    }
}
warning
The Risk of Mutability

Mutable DTOs can be modified unexpectedly after creation. Any code that holds a reference to the DTO can call a setter and change its state, leading to subtle bugs that are hard to trace, especially in multi-threaded environments.

And I used ModelMapper to map it to my JPA entity:

ModelMapper modelMapper = new ModelMapper();
User user = modelMapper.map(userDTO, User.class);

But here is the issue: DTOs should be immutable to make them thread-safe, predictable, and maintainable. So, I decided to replace my DTOs with Java Records.

Mutable POJO DTO
~25 lines
Requires no-arg constructor, getters, setters, and manual equals/hashCode. State can be changed after creation.
Java Record DTO
1 line
Immutable by default. Auto-generates constructor, getters, equals, hashCode, and toString.

The Power of Java Records

Since Java 14, we have records, and since I am using Java 21, it made perfect sense to adopt them.

Definition
Java Record

A record is a final, immutable class with automatic getters, a canonical constructor, equals(), hashCode(), and toString() methods. Records are designed specifically for carrying immutable data.

So, I refactored my DTO to:

public record UserDTO(String name, String email) {}

No setters. No boilerplate. Fully immutable.

auto_awesome
What You Get for Free

With a single line of code, Java Records give you: an all-args constructor, accessor methods (name() and email()), equals() and hashCode() based on all fields, and a clean toString() representation. All fields are private final by default.

Now, whenever I need a new DTO, I can just create a new instance, without worrying about accidental modifications.

But then, I ran into a new problem...

ModelMapper Does Not Support Java Records

When I tried using ModelMapper to convert my UserDTO record to a User entity, it threw an error because ModelMapper does not support Java records out of the box.

ModelMapper modelMapper = new ModelMapper();
User user = modelMapper.map(new UserDTO("John Doe", "john@example.com"), User.class);
key
Why ModelMapper Fails

ModelMapper relies on JavaBeans conventions - it expects a no-argument constructor and setter methods to populate the target object. Java Records have neither. They use a canonical constructor with all parameters, and their fields are final with no setters.

Why ModelMapper Breaks with Records
UserDTO (Record)→ModelMapper→No no-arg constructor!→Error!
ModelMapper expects JavaBeans conventions (no-arg constructor + setters) that records do not provide.

The Solution: modelmapper-module-record

After searching for a solution, I stumbled upon a StackOverflow answer that mentioned a new ModelMapper module for records: modelmapper-module-record.

Steps to Fix the Issue

Step 1
Add the Dependency
Add modelmapper-module-record to your build.gradle (or pom.xml).
Step 2
Register the RecordModule
In your Spring Boot configuration class, register the RecordModule with your ModelMapper bean.
Step 3
Use Records as DTOs
Replace your mutable POJO DTOs with Java Records and let ModelMapper handle the rest.

To enable record mapping, I added this dependency to build.gradle:

implementation 'org.modelmapper:modelmapper-module-record:1.0.0'

In my Spring Boot configuration class, I registered the RecordModule with ModelMapper:

import org.modelmapper.ModelMapper;
import org.modelmapper.module.record.RecordModule;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Bean;
import org.springframework.context.annotation.Configuration;

@Configuration
public class ModelMapperConfig {

    @Bean
    public ModelMapper modelMapper() {
        ModelMapper modelMapper = new ModelMapper();
        modelMapper.registerModule(new RecordModule()); // Enable Record Support
        return modelMapper;
    }
}
lightbulb
How the RecordModule Works

The RecordModule teaches ModelMapper how to create instances of Java Records by using the canonical constructor instead of the no-arg constructor + setter pattern. It inspects the record's component names and matches them to source properties automatically.

Final Working Code

Here is the complete Spring Boot setup:

DTO Using Java Record

public record UserDTO(String name, String email) {}

JPA Entity

import jakarta.persistence.*;

@Entity
public class User {
    @Id
    @GeneratedValue(strategy = GenerationType.IDENTITY)
    private Long id;
    private String name;
    private String email;

    // Getters and Setters
}

ModelMapper Configuration

@Configuration
public class ModelMapperConfig {

    @Bean
    public ModelMapper modelMapper() {
        ModelMapper modelMapper = new ModelMapper();
        modelMapper.registerModule(new RecordModule()); // Enable Record Support
        return modelMapper;
    }
}

Converting DTO to Entity

@Service
public class UserService {

    private final ModelMapper modelMapper;

    public UserService(ModelMapper modelMapper) {
        this.modelMapper = modelMapper;
    }

    public User convertToEntity(UserDTO userDTO) {
        return modelMapper.map(userDTO, User.class);
    }
}
Complete Mapping Flow
UserDTO (Record)→ModelMapper + RecordModule→User (Entity)
With the RecordModule registered, ModelMapper seamlessly converts immutable record DTOs to mutable JPA entities.

The Result

Now, when I call:

UserDTO dto = new UserDTO("John Doe", "john@example.com");
User user = modelMapper.map(dto, User.class);

It works flawlessly.

Key Takeaways

  1. Make your DTOs immutable. Java Records provide immutability, thread safety, and reduced boilerplate with a single line of code.
  2. ModelMapper needs help with Records. Add the modelmapper-module-record dependency and register the RecordModule to enable record support.
  3. Small change, big impact. Switching from mutable POJO DTOs to Java Records makes your codebase cleaner, safer, and more maintainable. If you are using Java 17+ and Spring Boot, this is a straightforward upgrade worth making.
auto_awesome
Bonus Tip

Java Records also work well with Jackson for JSON serialization/deserialization in Spring Boot REST APIs. Spring Boot's auto-configured ObjectMapper handles records natively, so you get immutable request and response bodies without any extra configuration.

Switching to Java Records for DTOs made my code cleaner, safer, and more maintainable. Thanks to ModelMapper's record module, mapping DTOs to JPA entities is now effortless. If you are using Java 17+ and Spring Boot, I highly recommend adopting Java Records for your DTOs.
